summary: Describes the SEED encryption algorithm, which is widely used in security systems in the Republic of Korea. It covers the encryption, the key scheduling, the S-boxes, and test vectors. It replaces RFC 4009. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: SEED is a symmetric block cipher described in this RFC. The document corrects unclear definitions from the earlier specification and adds examples that let implementers compare results.

subtitle: A clarified description of the SEED block cipher and its key schedule.

tldr.problem: RFC 4009 contained ambiguous definitions of parts of SEED, which could lead to incompatible implementations.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4269 gives corrected definitions and more detailed pseudocode for the cipher, its round function, and its key schedule. It also includes S-boxes and test vectors.
tldr.outcome: The clarification does not change the SEED algorithm itself. RFC 4269 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 4009.

today: RFC 4269 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 4009. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Changed in the Specification
sections.content:
SEED is a symmetric block cipher developed by the Korea Information Security Agency. The RFC describes its use in the Republic of Korea and specifies its encryption process, key schedule, S-boxes, and test vectors.

RFC 4269 obsoletes RFC 4009 because the earlier document had ambiguous function and SS-box definitions. This RFC corrects those definitions and provides fuller pseudocode; it explicitly says the SEED algorithm itself has not changed.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC clarifies how to implement SEED. It fixes unclear instructions without changing the cipher's algorithm.

sections.title: The 16-Round Feistel Structure
sections.content:
SEED takes a 128-bit input block and a 128-bit key. It divides the input into two 64-bit halves and applies a 16-round Feistel structure. In each round, a function uses one 64-bit subkey to transform one half and combine the result with the other half.

Decryption uses the encryption procedure with the round subkeys in reverse order. The round function uses S-boxes, permutations, XOR, and modular addition.
sections.plainLanguage: The cipher divides each block into two halves and processes them through sixteen rounds. Decryption repeats the process with the round keys in reverse order.

sections.title: Round Function and S-Boxes
sections.content:
The round function F takes a 64-bit input and divides it into two 32-bit parts. It combines those parts with two 32-bit subkey blocks and applies the function G in three layers.

Function G uses two 8-by-8 S-boxes and a permutation of sixteen 8-bit sub-blocks. The RFC also defines four extended SS-boxes that make the function faster at the cost of more memory.
sections.plainLanguage: The round function looks up values in two substitution tables and mixes them with the subkey. The RFC defines a larger set of tables for implementations that trade memory for speed.

sections.title: Generating Round Subkeys
sections.content:
The key schedule divides the 128-bit key into four 32-bit blocks and derives two 32-bit subkeys for each round. It uses function G, modular arithmetic, and a circular rotation of parts of the key.

After odd rounds, one pair of key blocks is rotated right by 8 bits. After even rounds, the other pair is rotated left by 8 bits. Appendix B gives test vectors with intermediate round values so an implementation can check its output.
sections.plainLanguage: The key schedule creates a different pair of subkeys for each round. Test vectors show expected intermediate and final values for sample inputs.
